    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24932v1</id>
    <title>Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:55:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24932v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24932v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24928v1</id>
    <title>Residual Allan Stability under Periodic Auxiliary Ramsey Sampling</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:54:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24928v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24928v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The timing of auxiliary Ramsey measurements can change the frequency stability associated with a drifting pulse shift at a fixed nominal Fisher-information rate for a constant shift. For periodic instantaneous observations of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck shift with causal prediction between updates, we derive the exact residual covariance averaged over the update cycle and the corresponding Allan variance at arbitrary averaging times. Relative to a continuous Kalman reference at the same information rate, periodic estimation increases the cycle-averaged estimation-error variance, reduces the short-time residual Allan variance, and increases its long-time value. Its covariance decays more slowly at the origin and has a larger integral. We extend the result to instantaneous sensing of the sum of finitely many independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck modes. Integrated observations preserve the short-time ordering for the scalar shift, and numerical calculations resolve the dependence of the crossover on window duration. A zero-order-hold comparison shows that the short-time ordering can change when the same estimator drives a different correction command. A three-level Ramsey model of coherent population trapping (CPT) maps the discriminator response to an effective information budget and illustrates how the dark times affect the choice of schedule.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24927v1</id>
    <title>Mapping the AI Supply Chain: Dependencies, Vulnerabilities, and Market Concentration in the AI Ecosystem</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:53:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24927v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24927v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain---highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk---then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24924v1</id>
    <title>Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:52:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24924v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24924v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. However, existing harness evolution methods often overlook implicit requirements and interaction needs, while using a single evolution agent to modify the harness and benchmark scores to select changes. This process often produces narrow patches and leads to benchmark-specific local optima. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered loop that brings real-world engineering practices into harness evolution. The loop consists of three steps: (1) User-driven evaluation lets simulated users raise their requirements as issues while they work with the harness over multiple turns. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. (3) Requirement-driven selection merges a change only when it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. Empirically, on held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% while using 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, and achieves higher pass@1 than Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE. In a blind human A/B test, real users prefer AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid pairs and rate it higher on all five dimensions, matching the directional preference of the user simulator. The human A/B results show that AHE-Beta achieves its goal of aligning harness evolution with real-world user requirements. Without further evolution, the gains transfer to GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with pass@1 improvements of 15.8% and 5.3% over Base Harness. Together, these results show that requirement-centered harness evolution is a more general method for improving agent capabilities.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24911v1</id>
    <title>A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:46:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24911v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24911v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>An effective theory of open quantum systems should preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and remain accurate throughout relaxation. Meeting both requirements is particularly challenging in quantum many-body systems, where dense spectra can invalidate the secular approximation even at weak coupling. Here we construct a nonsecular quantum master equation that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. Under suitable conditions, we prove a time-uniform $O(λ^2)$ bound on the difference between the predicted and exact reduced density matrices, where $λ$ is the system-bath coupling strength. Our construction completes the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance. In this approach, TR-KMS detailed balance is compatible with resonance matching, whereas its counterpart without time reversal is not. In a benchmark against the exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, our equation maintains $O(λ^2)$ accuracy across secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming the existing detailed-balance equations tested. These results provide a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24910v1</id>
    <title>Dressed-State Quantum Information Processing Using a Multilayer Ion Trap Chip with an Integrated Radio Frequency Resonator</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:44:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24910v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24910v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We present the experimental preparation of a radio frequency (RF)-dressed-state qubit, the coherent operation of a single RF-dressed qubit, and the selective readout of RF-dressed hyperfine states of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions trapped using a novel microstructured ion trap chip. We demonstrate the individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. To this end, we developed, manufactured, and characterized a trap chip specifcally designed for quantum information processing with RF-dressed-state qubits. The chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated resonator that creates a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude along the axis of a linear ion crystal. This RF gradient enables the individual addressing of dressed qubit states as well as their coupling. We characterize the ion trap chip experimentally using the hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of laser cooled $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions and by applying a single, global, modulated RF field oscillating near 12.6 GHz that drives dressed-state resonances.
  We present a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip specifically designed for quantum information processing based on dressed-state qubits. This ion trap chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated radio frequency (RF) resonator, creating a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude that allows for individual qubit addressing and qubit-qubit coupling. We experimentally characterize this ion trap chip demonstrating dressed-qubit state preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and dressed-state-selective read-out using hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$. For this purpose, a global modulated RF driving field oscillating near 12.6 GHz is applied to the ions. In addition, we demonstrate individual addressing of dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24908v1</id>
    <title>Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:43:40Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24908v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24908v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.</summary>

    <title>Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:37:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24896v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24896v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24892v1</id>
    <title>On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:34:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24892v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24892v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24891v1</id>
    <title>Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:34:10Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24891v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24891v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24890v1</id>
    <title>Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:32:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24890v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24890v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Symmetry-preserving (SP) variational quantum circuits restrict evolution to physically relevant sectors of Hilbert space, but symmetry preservation alone does not guarantee accessibility within those sectors. We show that a restricted generator set can possess a residual dynamical Lie algebra whose commutant further decomposes the target symmetry sector into invariant blocks. The associated block populations are conserved and impose a kinematic upper bound on the fidelity with a target state. We then invert this diagnostic into a circuit-design principle: candidate SP generators can be screened before variational optimization by asking whether they break the residual commutant, which invariant blocks they couple, and what adjoint module they generate under the residual algebra. For two orthogonal residual blocks we prove that a single elementary real inter-block rotation generates the full orthogonal algebra. We further derive a complex escape criterion: if the real and imaginary parts of an inter-block seed are independent over the residual intertwiner algebra, the generated module is the full complex coupling space and the enlarged algebra becomes special unitary. A connected residual-block graph yields a natural multi-block generalization and suggests minimum-cost spanning-tree circuit design. We demonstrate this design principle in the XXZ and Hubbard models, where residual-algebra screening identifies SP circuit extensions that remove the relevant accessibility obstructions. These examples establish a unified route from residual-symmetry diagnosis and fidelity bounds to predictive quantum circuit design.</summary>

    <title>Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:32:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24888v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24888v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.</summary>

    <title>CREST: A Hardware-Aware GNN-Based Framework for High-Fidelity and Robust Superconducting Quantum Compilation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:31:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24886v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24886v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum compilation on superconducting processors requires selecting a connected execution region whose topology and calibrated properties suit the input circuit. This choice constrains subsequent routing and influences the noise encountered during execution, yet aggregate hardware-quality metrics alone may not reliably predict the execution fidelity of a given circuit. Calibration updates can also change region suitability and trigger the rebuilding of calibration-dependent resource structures. We present CREST, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework that evaluates circuit-region compatibility before routing. It encodes gate dependencies and logical-qubit interactions alongside each candidate region's connectivity and current calibration attributes; bidirectional cross-graph attention relates the two representations, while real-device execution outcomes supervise candidate ranking. The trained scorer is reused with updated calibration attributes. Evaluations on 324 circuits from seven datasets on TianYan-176 show that CREST improves mean measurement-distribution fidelity by 19.03% over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest mean fidelity on every dataset. Furthermore, using updated calibration attributes, the same trained model maintains the highest overall mean fidelity across six measurement dates without retraining. With a unified model of circuit-region compatibility, CREST improves execution fidelity across diverse workloads and sustains that advantage as hardware calibration changes.</summary>

    <title>Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:29:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24885v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24885v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.</summary>

    <title>Hurst Exponent Estimation with Quantum Wavelets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:28:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24882v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24882v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>How accurately can the Hurst exponent $H$ of fractional Brownian motion be estimated from repeated preparations of a single amplitude-encoded path, when every measurement interrogates the same realization? We extend the $ε$-decimated quantum nondecimated wavelet transform in three directions: we remove the endpoint jump of circular filtering, derive the sampling distribution of the estimator, and compare readouts at equal query budgets. A one-qubit mirror extension removes the jump and keeps every coefficient that straddles a fold of the same order as an interior coefficient, for any compactly supported filter and circular shift. The transform for any such filter is compiled from the paraunitary lattice of its filter bank, and the energy share of a level is the success probability of one multiply-controlled reflection, which is both the controlled unitary of a Hadamard test and the oracle of amplitude estimation. For filters with at least two vanishing moments we prove a root-$N$ central limit theorem for the log-energy contrasts, independent of the limiting path norm, so the studentized estimator is asymptotically standard normal for deterministic query budgets under which the success count at every level diverges. For sparse counts we give a working multinomial--lognormal likelihood, exact in its readout model for direct measurement, and check its coverage by simulation. For paths of length $512$, mirroring reduces RMSE by a factor of $3$--$10$ for $H\ge0.5$, and with exact shares the nondecimated db2 estimator is $6$--$14\%$ above the root Cramér--Rao bound. Hadamard level tests are less accurate than direct measurement of the leading qubits at every budget. At $H=0.9$ and $2^{20}$ queries, maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation attains RMSE $0.0347$, against $0.0451$ for direct measurement and $0.0295$ with exact shares.</summary>

    <title>Monoculture Robust Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:27:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24881v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24881v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is $ρ$-replicable, then running it independently $k$ times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with $k$, controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and $ρ$. We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to $γ$ can require a sample-size multiplier of $t = Ω(\log(1/γ))$.</summary>

    <title>Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:27:40Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24880v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24880v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.</summary>

    <title>Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:24:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24877v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24877v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.</summary>

    <summary>Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.</summary>

    <title>TangentPDE: Learning Local Operator Responses with Sparse Finite-Difference Supervision</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:23:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24873v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24873v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neural PDE operators are often optimized through state reconstruction, which largely constrains operator values at observed inputs but does not fully characterize their sensitivity to local perturbations. A more faithful approximation of operator behavior requires not only accurate state predictions, but also correct variations along local perturbation directions. We present TangentPDE, which uses finite differences to approximate directional derivatives and constructs task-relevant finite-step responses from the state outputs of a reference solver at sparse paired inputs. Its objective jointly constrains state fidelity, response-direction alignment, and response-magnitude calibration, thereby learning both operator values and their local variations. Because the response labels are constructed solely from state outputs at paired inputs, the method requires neither explicit derivative labels, linearized or adjoint PDE solves, nor full Jacobians, and remains applicable to nonlinear solvers without derivative interfaces. Building on this, we additionally propose a selectively executed adaptation mechanism to strengthen local operator representations under finite-difference supervision. Budget-matched and correspondence-perturbed controls isolate the effect of relational supervision from improvements attributable to additional state observations or increased data volume. Designed as a plug-and-play training framework, TangentPDE integrates with diverse neural-operator backbones. Across four PDE systems and 20 task-backbone settings, TangentPDE lowers the three-seed mean state error in 18 settings and the corresponding Rollout@20 error in 18, while intrinsic finite-step response gains are strongest on DiffReact and remain task- and backbone-dependent elsewhere.</summary>

    <title>WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:20:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24869v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24869v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.</summary>

    <title>Time-Varying Medium from an Ensemble of Laser-Dressed Quantum Emitters</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:18:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24861v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24861v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We propose a minimal quantum-mechanical model of a frequency dispersive, time-modulated medium that explicitly incorporates the pumping mechanism. It consists of a homogeneous ensemble of quantum emitters dressed by a pump laser. We analyze their dispersive, time-varying response to a perturbative probe field by deriving the macroscopic polarizability of the ensemble, and then solving Maxwell's equations via the Floquet formalism. This yields a rich band structure that departs from conventional analyses in which the modulation source is neglected, arising from the interplay between the dispersive polaritonic and time-varying responses. These results shed light on the role of the modulation source in time-varying media and pave the way toward realizing dispersive time-varying media from driven quantum-mechanical systems.</summary>

    <title>The limits of magic-state cultivation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:11:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24852v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24852v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Fault tolerance is understood through Pauli algebra, which fails at non-Clifford gates. Circuits such as magic-state cultivation, which checks an encoded T state with physical T gates, have therefore lacked an exact theory of which faults are harmful. We develop such a theory and show that, for any circuit that prepares a magic state with non-Clifford gates and postselection, one stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates decides which faults are harmful. This ties cultivation to distillation, bounds its T-count from below and gives an exact test. For a single check on an ideally encoded state, the fault distance reduces to Pauli algebra on the code. As a use case, we analyze the S gates that have stood in for T gates in the design of cultivation. We show that this proxy can only overstate the fault distance of such a check, and that the checks in use, on color and surface codes, tolerate at most half as many faults as their code allows. The theory also yields nearest-neighbor checks that keep the full distance, certified up to code distance nine.</summary>

    <title>Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:08:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24846v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24846v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.</summary>

    <title>Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:07:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24845v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24845v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.</summary>

    <title>General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:07:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24844v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24844v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.</summary>

    <title>Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:07:43Z</updated>

    <summary>Neural surrogates for external vehicle aerodynamics are fast alternatives to physics-based computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. Their foundational limitation is a lack of zero-shot generalization across vehicle classes, which results in an expensive, custom training campaign for each new vehicle design. Similar to pretrained models in other fields, a pretrained surrogate should adapt to a new vehicle class using only a few simulations and stay accurate on its pretraining domain. No prior study has systematically tested this transfer behavior. We conduct a large-scale, controlled benchmarking study on five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates across four independent target datasets. These datasets differ from the source in geometry, CFD solver, turbulence model, and flow conditions. We find that fine-tuning these surrogates outperforms training from scratch in fewer than half of the comparisons and lowers the accuracy of the surrogate on its source dataset. We introduce GeoReplay, a geometry- and gradient-aligned source replay that keeps source simulations resembling the target in training and applies their updates only when they agree with the target gradient. A risk bound separates geometric coverage from differences in the simulated physics, and we prove that every sufficiently small GeoReplay step decreases the target training objective. GeoReplay lowers the source error of fine-tuning in 77 of 80 settings and matches its target accuracy.</summary>

    <title>Does the Action Matter? Probing Action-Conditioned Semantic Forecasting as a World Model for Autonomous Driving</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:06:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24840v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24840v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.</summary>

    <title>Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:05:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24839v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24839v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>One popular architecture for multi-agent systems (MAS) relies on an orchestrator that generates an initial plan, coordinates its execution, and dynamically revises the plan based on agent feedback when tasks cannot be fully specified in advance. This dynamic replanning introduces a critical vulnerability: malicious agents can embed instructions within their feedback to hijack the replanning process. Existing defenses focus exclusively on per-tool access control or static, pre-execution policy enforcement, leaving the replanning phase unsecured.
  We introduce Kaer, a multi-agent framework featuring security-aware replanning. Kaer shields the planner from untrusted agent feedback by conveying diagnostics to the replanning procedure strictly through abstract templates. Plan revisions are restricted to a set of deterministic repair operators, and all modified plans must satisfy preset policies. We create Cintra, a benchmark of simulated user tasks requiring replanning paired with adversarial objectives targeting the replanning phase. Using Cintra, we evaluate both task completion rates and system vulnerability to replanning exploits by malicious agents. Evaluating Kaer on Cintra against Magentic-One (an undefended MAS) and ControlValve (the state-of-the-art defense) demonstrates that Kaer achieves higher robustness than both systems while maintaining comparable utility to ControlValve. Although abstract failure templates slightly constrain utility on select tasks, Kaer enables MAS to perform secure, dynamic plan revisions without exposing the orchestrator to untrusted agent feedback.</summary>

    <title>What Survival Benchmarks Don't Tell You: Impact of Model Selection and Dataset Regimes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:03:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24837v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24837v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Despite the proliferation of survival analysis methods, current benchmarks often operate under narrow conditions: they heavily rely on the concordance index (C-index) for evaluation and model selection, and frequently either exclude deep learning (DL) methods or underrepresent challenging dataset regimes. To address these limitations, we conduct a large-scale, neutral benchmark comparing 10 classical, tree-based, and DL methods across 49 diverse datasets. Crucially, we treat the model selection criterion (optimizing for C-index, Integrated Brier Score (IBS), or Mean Absolute Error (MAE-PO)) as an independent experimental variable. Using Bayesian mixed-effects modeling, we demonstrate that evaluation design heavily dictates conclusions. For complex DL and tree-based architectures, selecting hyperparameters to optimize for IBS instead of C-index yields substantial improvements in probabilistic accuracy and calibration at a negligible cost to discriminative ranking. Furthermore, method performance (C-index, IBS, MAE-PO, and X-CAL) is fundamentally governed by dataset characteristics. While DL models scale exceptionally well with larger sample sizes, they suffer notable performance drops in high-dimensional feature spaces. Additionally, we expose a structural vulnerability where heavy censoring artificially inflates absolute calibration metrics, creating overly conservative tests. Ultimately, our findings challenge the utility of global single-number performance summaries and advocate for survival analysis results that transparently report the evaluation setup. Our code is available at: https://github.com/sdening/surv-bench-study</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24834v1</id>
    <title>Shedding Light on Quantum Non-Classicality: Witnessing Wigner Negativity with Free Electrons</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:01:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24834v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24834v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Certifying quantum non-classicality like Wigner negativity typically demands full optical state tomography. This work introduces a noise-resilient framework for witnessing optical Wigner negativity using phase-resolved quantum photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (QPINEM). By mapping electron coherences directly to symmetrically ordered optical characteristic functions within a coupling-limited phase-space region, the protocol bypasses full optical reconstruction. A post-measurement witness matrix is constructed via Bochner's theorem from recorded electron spectra, where negative eigenvalues certify non-classicality. To ensure reliability under realistic experimental conditions, a noise-aware selection procedure decouples discovery from statistical validation. Benchmarked across various optical preparations-including vacuum-Fock superpositions, odd cat states, and GKP states-the protocol provides a statistically bounded pathway for probing quantum features with free electrons.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24831v1</id>
    <title>Overlooked and Underutilized: Prototypes are the Missing Piece in Tabular XAI</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:00:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24831v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24831v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.</summary>

    <title>A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T17:59:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24830v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24830v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24827v1</id>
    <title>Synthesizing hyperspectral Data using generative Models to train spectral Unmixing Methods for low-cost Crop Residue Cover Mapping</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T17:58:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24827v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24827v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The spectral range of the Field Imaging Nanosatellite for Crop residue Hyperspectral Mapping (FINCH), developed by the University of Toronto Aerospace Team's Space System Division, poses significant challenges for hyperspectral unmixing to determine crop residue cover fractional abundances. The severe lack of standard indices necessitates the use of complex, data-driven unmixing models. Complex unmixing models require dense, well-distributed manifolds, whereas ground-truth datasets are sparse and expensive. To better leverage the information content in existing ground-truth datasets, this study presents a framework that decouples interpolation and abundance-mapping estimation via an intermediary conditional data generator, contrasting with traditional single-model unmixing pipelines. This decoupling enables the inclusion of physical prior knowledge about spectra, which is not natively accessible to unmixing models, thereby artificially expanding the dataset to serve as a Monte Carlo approximation of the population risk. To test this hypothesis, we have proposed two generator models: a 1D Conditional U-Net with Conformer Layers (GD-Streamline) and a Dual-Path Transformer Conditional Variational AutoEncoder (TCVAE), and two unmixing models: Multi-Layered Perceptrons (MLP) and Fourier Neural Operators (FNO). The results of the study indicate a need for rigorous integration and introduction of spectral priors within the scope of the proposed decoupling framework to prevent domain and mode collapse and hallucination by the generator models; otherwise, this leads to falsely approximated data manifolds, ultimately resulting in unsatisfactory and out-of-distribution unmixing performance.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24810v1</id>
    <title>LAaDT-DSS: decision support for non-experts on rooftop PV, incentive and grid simulations under Turkish tariff rules</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T17:45:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24810v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24810v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Rooftop photovoltaics raise three questions: should a household invest, which incentive costs the state least, and does the feeder stay within limits? Those who ask are rarely modellers. We present LAaDT-DSS, decision-support software that answers all three under Turkish tariff rules from one simulation core. Non-experts reach it by clicking a house on a 3D map or by asking in plain words; a language model is asked to call the simulation tools, not to compute. Each entry of its 125-entry parameter registry is marked as sourced or estimated. Case studies test the system. Its PV yield lies within $\pm$3.6% of two independent tools at equal losses. Across 2,048 draws of its estimated inputs, the answer for PV alone held in all but one; with a battery, it changed in 31-41% of the draws. Four scripted chat scenarios ran end to end; no user study was run.</summary>

    <title>Prognosis Without Prediction: The Intrinsic Geometry of Survival</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T17:42:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24799v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24799v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Modeling systemic failure in high-dimensional environments is fundamentally limited by supervised algorithms that attempt to predict sparse, noisy or censored endpoints. To break this reliance on explicit outcome regression, we engineered the Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM) framework, a deep learning architecture that decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels and treats time-to-event progression as an emergent geometric property. The system projects heterogeneous multi-omics arrays into a unified latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows. To validate the framework, we applied this architecture to a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort. Across a deterministic 5-fold cross-validation pipeline, SOSM achieved a mean Concordance Index of $0.768 \pm 0.068$, while out-of-fold risk stratification yielded significant survival divergence (log-rank $p < 0.001$) accompanied by a 14.7% increase in local manifold dissipation among high-risk patients. Furthermore, interrogating the network's encoder weights confirmed that the model autonomously recovered canonical metabolic and microenvironmental drivers of disease progression without supervised feature selection. By demonstrating that systemic failure can be mapped as a geometric phase transition, SOSM establishes a generalizable computational engine for prognostic modeling across biological, industrial and financial complex systems.</summary>

    <title>Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T17:41:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24798v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24798v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24797v1</id>
    <title>Bias-Only Training Dynamics in ReLU Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T17:41:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24797v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24797v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neural networks with randomly initialized, fixed weights and trainable biases are universal approximators, yet the dynamics of bias-only training remain largely unexplored. We study these dynamics in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks through activation codes, the binary patterns of active neurons that partition the input space into convex polyhedral regions. We show that the gradients with respect to the biases depend on each input only through its activation code, and hence the training dynamics can be characterized with these codes. In particular, as long as the activation codes remain fixed, training reduces to a linear least-squares problem with the codes as features. Training can then be understood as a sequence of least-squares problems, with transitions occurring when neurons change their activation states. We show that the fraction of switching neurons vanishes as the network widens, and the training dynamics approach those of linear least squares on the initial activation codes in the infinite-width limit. Our experiments support these theoretical findings, showing that while activation switches can noticeably affect training in narrower networks, their relative frequency and the associated changes in the dynamics diminish as the width increases.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24793v1</id>
    <title>The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T17:38:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24793v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24793v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/V-lens.</summary>

1. Male or female ≥ 18 years of age.
2. Participants have received at least one prior line of standard-of-care treatment for high-grade glioma (HGG). Specifically, participants have received prior surgery that resulted in histopathologic diagnosis followed by treatment with radiation alone and/or radiation plus temozolomide.
3. Participants with recurrent high-grade glioma (rHGG) for whom resection is planned, and with a lesion that is accessible to convection-enhanced delivery (CED) therapy. Eligible tumor types include central nervous system (CNS) World Health Organization (WHO) Grade 4 astrocytoma isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) wild-type (WT) (i.e., glioblastoma), WHO Grade 4 astrocytoma IDH mutated, WHO Grade 3 astrocytoma IDH WT or mutated, and WHO Grade 3 oligodendroglioma IDH mutated, 1p19q codeleted. Participants may have had multiple recurrences.
4. Tumors must be supratentorial in location, and participants can only have a single lesion that is ≥ 1 centimeter and ≤ 4 centimeters in diameter.
5. Performance Level using the Karnofsky score ≥ 70%. Note: Neurologic deficits in participants with CNS tumors must have been stable for at least 7 days with no new deficits prior to study enrollment. Participants who are unable to walk because of paralysis, but who are up in a wheelchair, will be considered ambulatory for the purpose of assessing the Karnofsky performance score.
6. Predictable life expectancy of at least 3 months.
7. Participants must have adequately recovered from the acute toxic effects of all prior anti-cancer chemotherapy and must be at least 3 weeks from previous cytotoxic chemotherapy, 4 weeks from prior radiation therapy, and at least 2 weeks from any major surgery, with evidence of adequate wound healing.
8. Participants must have adequate organ function based on laboratory assessments obtained within 21 days prior to study treatment. Laboratory values obtained as part of standard of care within this timeframe may be used to satisfy eligibility criteria.

   Adequate bone marrow function:

   absolute neutrophil count ≥1,500/microliter (mcL) platelets ≥100,000/mcL

   Adequate hepatic function:

   total bilirubin ≤ 2x upper limit of normal (ULN) for their age Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT) ≤2 X institutional upper limit of normal alanine aminotransferase (ALT) serum glutamic-pyruvic transaminase (SGPT) ≤2 X institutional upper limit of normal Serum albumin ≥ 2 g/dL

   Adequate renal function:

   creatinine ≤ 1.5 x within institutional upper limit of normal OR creatinine clearance radioisotope (GFR) ≥ 70 mL/min/1.73 m2, calculated using the Cockcroft-Gault equation, unless data exists supporting safe use at lower kidney function values, no lower than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2

   Adequate coagulation:

   Prothrombin time and international normalized ratio ≤ 1.5x ULN

   Note: Participants receiving anticoagulant therapy must be able to safely discontinue anticoagulation per institutional guidelines and the treating neurosurgeon's discretion prior to infusion of SRN-101.
9. Participants with seizure disorders may be enrolled if on a stable anticonvulsant dose and not experiencing refractory seizures in the last 3 months.
10. Agree to participate in the long-term safety follow-up.
11. Ability to understand and the willingness to sign a written informed consent document.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Disseminated disease or multifocal disease.
2. Pregnant or breastfeeding. Participants of childbearing potential and male participants with female partners of childbearing potential must agree to always use highly effective forms of contraception during the course of the study and for at least 3 months after completion of study intervention. Contraceptive use by participants should be consistent with local regulations regarding the methods of contraception for those participating in clinical studies. Participants of childbearing potential must have a negative blood pregnancy test within 21 days of commencement of study intervention. Participants must refrain from donating sperm during the course of the study and for at least 3 months after completion of study intervention.
3. History of active liver disease, including Hepatitis B or Hepatitis C or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
4. Another concurrent tumor immunotherapy.
5. Initiation and/or escalation of systemic immunosuppressive therapy (including corticosteroids) within 7 days prior to study initiation, except protocol-required peri-procedural dexamethasone. Participants already on dexamethasone (at a maximum dose of 4 mg per day) are eligible.
6. Known or suspected hypersensitivity to Gadoteridol, its excipients, or other gadolinium-based contrast agents.
7. Recent onset of neurologic dysfunction or abnormality that is deemed by the Investigator to prevent patient participation.
8. Inability, or potential inability, to comply with the safety monitoring requirements of the study, as determined by the Investigator's opinion.
9. Other comorbidities that the Investigator believes will negatively impact the participant's ability to benefit from or tolerate this study.
10. Inability to undergo an MRI.
11. * Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) Performance Status of 0 or 1
* Life expectancy ≥ 3 months, as determined by the investigator
* Histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma originating from the colon or rectum
* Metastatic disease not amenable to local treatment
* Disease progression during or following not more than two separate lines of treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) that consisted of fluoropyrimidine-, oxaliplatin-, and irinotecan-containing chemotherapy in combination with a biologic agent
* Measurable disease (at least one target lesion) according to RECIST v1.1
* Adequate hematologic and end-organ function obtained within 14 days prior to initiation of study treatment

Exclusion Criteria:

* High microsatellite instability (MSI-H) tumor
* Presence of BRAFV600E mutation
* Prior treatment with any of the protocol-specified study treatments
* Prior treatment with T-cell co-stimulating or immune checkpoint blockade therapies including anti-CTLA-4, anti-PD-1, and anti-PD-L1 therapeutic antibodies
* Biologic treatment within 2 weeks prior to initiation of study treatment, or other systemic treatment for CRC within 2 weeks or 5 half-lives of the drug (whichever is shorter) prior to initiation of study treatment
* Treatment with investigational therapy within 28 days prior to initiation of study treatment
* Eligibility only for the control arm
* Prior allogeneic stem cell or solid organ transplantation
* Treatment with systemic immunostimulatory agents within 4 weeks or 5 half-lives of the drug (whichever is longer) prior to the initiation of study treatment
* Treatment with systemic immunosuppressive medication within 2 weeks prior to initiation of study treatment, or anticipation of need for systemic immunosuppressant medication during study treatment
* Treatment with a live, attenuated vaccine within 4 weeks prior to initiation of study treatment, or anticipation of need for such a vaccine during atezolizumab treatment or within 5 months after the last dose of atezolizumab
* Current treatment with anti-viral therapy for HBV
* Uncontrolled pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, ascites requiring recurrent drainage procedures (once monthly or more frequently), or tumor related-pain,
* Uncontrolled or symptomatic hypercalcemia (ionized calcium \>1.5 mmol/L, calcium \>12 mg/dL, or corrected serum calcium \>ULN)
* Symptomatic, untreated, or actively progressing CNS metastases
* History of leptomeningeal disease
* Active or history of autoimmune disease or immune deficiency
* History of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, organizing pneumonia, drug-induced pneumonitis, or idiopathic pneumonitis, or evidence of active pneumonitis on screening chest computed tomography (CT) scan
* History of malignancy other than CRC within 2 years prior to screening, with the exception of malignancies with a negligible risk of metastasis or death
* Active tuberculosis
* Severe infection within 4 weeks prior to initiation of study treatment
